rationale: Full text examined (11 pages). Das and Walton (2015) combine random-sample household survey data (1,200 households across four localities, settlement censuses, and quantitative supplement tables) with multi-year ethnographic interviews and court-record analysis (mixed_methods) to compare struggles over housing and urban infrastructure in two unplanned settlements in Delhi's National Capital Region (Punjabi Basti and NOIDA Sectors 5 and 8). Multiple rule-type mechanisms co-equally structure these struggles: eligibility_status_documentation is the single most pervasive focal mechanism (legal settlement tenure categories, sequential house numbering and an authorized neighborhood map required for metering and colony regularization in Punjabi Basti, and official eligibility surveys, contested beneficiary lists, and ration/voter ID residency documentation in NOIDA), alongside co-central review_redress (civil litigation against Ramjas Foundation and Allahabad High Court stay orders and writ petitions for resettlement), participation_assistance (local political leaders and registered societies navigating bureaucracy), and regulatory_model_ownership / enforcement_sanctions (electricity privatization under BSES and police complaints for electricity theft). The focal empirical outcomes analyzed in the main text are administrative and governance outcomes (administrative_outcome)—official map approval, provisional colony authorization, formal meter regularization, court stay orders against demolition, enumeration on official resettlement lists, and local political leadership structures—while ongoing water and sewage infrastructure projects are noted as open questions rather than evaluated as primary WASH access outcomes in the text.
